memo: After reviewing the financial impact of each possible path for the 125 roles that can be automated, the elimination option delivers the greatest long‑term value for shareholders.  The AI tools will replace 25% of the work in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations, so the company can safely remove all 125 positions.  By eliminating these roles we retain the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits savings while incurring a one‑time severance expense of $1.1 million.  This yields a net cash inflow of $10.3 million in the first year and $11.4 million every subsequent year.  Over a 20‑year horizon the cumulative benefit exceeds $220 million, far surpassing the modest savings from retraining paths, which involve significant upfront training costs and ongoing higher payroll.  The decision also aligns with the board’s mandate to maximize shareholder value, preserves cash (the $44.1 million excess operating cash comfortably covers the severance), and maintains a lean cost structure for the remaining workforce.  Therefore, we will eliminate all 125 positions, pay the required severance, and reallocate the saved resources to growth initiatives and shareholder returns.

The AI automation of office‑admin and business‑finance work makes those 125 roles redundant.  Eliminating them delivers the greatest long‑term shareholder value.  The one‑time severance outlay is $1.1 million, a negligible cost compared with the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits that will be removed.  Over a 20‑year horizon the net cash benefit exceeds $220 million (ignoring discounting), far outstripping the modest savings from retraining paths.  The cash required to fund severance is covered by the $44.1 million cash cushion above the operating minimum, leaving ample liquidity and preserving the company’s strong debt‑to‑EBITDA (2.3×) and interest‑coverage (7.4×) ratios.  By eliminating the roles we also improve operating margin, return on equity and free cash flow, supporting higher dividends and share‑repurchase capacity for shareholders.  No retraining costs or ongoing pay differentials are incurred, and the plant workforce remains unchanged, as the AI solution fully replaces the functions.  Therefore, we allocate all 125 affected employees to the “eliminate” path.

The AI assessment shows that 25% of the work in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations can be fully automated, covering 125 roles. To maximize shareholder value over the next twenty years, the most financially advantageous option is to eliminate these positions. The annual payroll and benefits cost of these roles is $11.4 million; eliminating them removes this recurring expense. The one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million is modest relative to the annual cash savings and can be funded from the $44.1 million cash buffer above the minimum operating level. No retraining costs are incurred, and the company avoids the additional $2.1 million per year that would arise from keeping current pay in a plant role. Moreover, eliminating the roles does not affect production capacity because the work is now performed by AI. The net effect is an immediate cash outflow of $1.1 million and a sustained annual cash flow improvement of $11.4 million, enhancing operating margin, free cash flow, and return on equity, thereby delivering the greatest long‑term value to shareholders.

After reviewing the board’s objective of maximizing shareholder value over the next twenty years, the most financially advantageous option is to eliminate all 125 roles in office‑and‑administrative support and business‑and‑financial operations that can be replaced by AI. The AI solution can cover 25% of the work in these functions, which corresponds exactly to the 125 positions (70 in office support and 55 in business/financial ops). Eliminating these roles removes the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits expense, while the one‑time severance cost of $1.1 million is easily covered by the $44.1 million cash buffer above the minimum operating level. No retraining costs are incurred, preserving cash for other strategic investments. Moving staff to plant roles or keeping them at current pay would generate additional ongoing costs (training outlays and higher payroll) that do not improve cash flow. Therefore, we allocate the full 125 people to the elimination path, with zero allocations to the retraining paths, delivering the greatest long‑term cash‑flow benefit and supporting the board’s shareholder‑value mandate.

The AI automation can replace 25% of the work in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations, eliminating the need for 125 roles. By terminating these positions we capture the full $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits saving, while incurring a one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million – well within the $44.1 million cash buffer. No ongoing payroll or retraining costs are required, and we avoid the $5.7 million training expense and the $2.1 million annual supplement needed if employees were retrained and kept at current pay. The net effect is an immediate cash‑flow improvement of roughly $10.3 million and a permanent reduction in operating expenses, which lifts operating margin, ROE and free cash flow. Over a 20‑year horizon the present value of the annual $11.4 million savings far exceeds the modest severance cost, delivering clear shareholder value. Consequently, we eliminate all 125 affected employees, leveraging the automation gains to strengthen the balance sheet and enhance long‑term returns.

After a detailed financial analysis of the three possible paths for the 125 affected employees, the elimination route delivers the greatest shareholder value over the next twenty years. Eliminating the roles incurs a one‑time severance cost of $1.1 million, but it removes the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits expense associated with these positions, generating a net cash flow improvement of roughly $10.3 million in the first year and $11.4 million every subsequent year. The alternative retraining options require a $7.6 million upfront investment and either provide only a modest $2.1 million annual payroll reduction (move_plant_pay) or add a $2.1 million annual cost (move_keep_pay). Even when considering the $44.1 million cash buffer above the minimum operating level, the elimination path maximizes cash generation, improves the debt‑to‑EBITDA ratio, and enhances return on equity without compromising the Company’s operational capacity, as the plant roles can be filled by external hires. Therefore, we will eliminate all 125 positions, pay the required severance, and redeploy the saved resources to higher‑return initiatives for shareholders.

The Board’s mandate is to create long‑term shareholder value.  The three available pathways differ sharply in cash impact and ongoing cost.  Eliminating a role provides the greatest immediate cash savings – a one‑time severance of $8,902 per person and a permanent payroll reduction of roughly $71,800 per year (the weighted average of office‑admin and finance staff).  Moving staff to a plant role at the plant’s pay level also yields a net cash benefit: a one‑time retraining outlay of $60,600 per person, offset after two years by the lower annual payroll ($55,200 versus $71,800) and by avoiding the external hiring expense the plants would otherwise incur for the 500 annual hires.  Keeping current pay after retraining adds a recurring $16,560 per person and therefore erodes value; it is not justified without a strategic reason that does not exist here.

Accordingly, we eliminate 80 positions – the largest feasible slice that maximises cash flow while still preserving a pool of internal talent for plant needs.  The remaining 45 employees are retrained and transferred to plant roles at the plant pay rate, reducing external hiring costs and delivering a modest annual payroll saving of $745k.  No employees are placed on the keep‑pay path.  The total one‑time outlay ($3.44 M) is comfortably covered by the $44.1 M cash cushion, and the combined annual payroll reduction ($6.49 M) strengthens free cash flow, supporting dividends, repurchases and future growth initiatives over the next twenty years.

The board’s 20‑year value‑creation mandate requires us to prioritize actions that generate the greatest net cash benefit while preserving the Company’s operational capacity.  Eliminating roles delivers the largest immediate cash‑flow gain: each of the 95 eliminated employees saves an average of $71,771 in annual payroll (including benefits) and incurs a one‑time severance cost of $8,902.  Over a 20‑year horizon this translates to roughly $1.4 billion of payroll savings, far outweighing the $845 k total severance outlay.

We retain a modest cohort (30 people) for retraining into plant positions at the plant‑role pay of $55,211.  The $60,600 one‑time retraining expense per person is recovered within two years when compared with the cost of hiring external workers for the same roles, and the move reduces annual payroll by $16,560 per person.  This not only cuts ongoing labor costs but also lessens the need for external hires, supporting plant productivity and protecting margins.

The “move‑keep‑pay” option adds a recurring $16,560 per employee in salary over the plant pay, offering no net cash benefit and therefore is excluded.  By allocating 95 eliminations and 30 retrain‑to‑plant moves, we maximize cash generation, maintain sufficient internal talent for the plants, and align with the long‑term shareholder‑value objective.
